lab_title: Vectors and Projectile Motion: From Components to Trajectories
top_level_objectives: Represent quantities with magnitude and direction using vectors, and add two vectors graphically using the tip-to-tail method to find a resultant.
Decompose a vector into horizontal (x) and vertical (y) components and relate its magnitude and direction to those components using right-triangle trigonometry.
Explain that the horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile are independent, with constant horizontal velocity and uniformly accelerated vertical velocity.
Predict and observe how launch angle and initial speed determine a projectile's trajectory, range, and maximum height.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce vectors as objects carrying both magnitude and direction, distinguishing them from plain numbers (scalars), to establish the conceptual foundation for the lab.
key_visuals: A single glowing arrow floating in AR space with an adjustable length (magnitude) and orientation (direction)
A readout panel displaying the vector's magnitude and angle as the arrow changes
Side-by-side contrast of a scalar quantity (a number) versus a vector quantity (an arrow)
student_actions: Grab the arrow's tip and drag it to change its length and direction, watching the magnitude and angle readout update
Sort a small set of example quantities (e.g., temperature, velocity, mass, displacement) into 'scalar' or 'vector' bins

scenes.brief_purpose: Teach graphical vector addition so students see how two vectors combine into a single resultant, reinforcing that order does not change the outcome.
key_visuals: Two colored arrows that can be slid so the tail of one meets the tip of the other
A dashed resultant arrow drawn from the start of the first vector to the tip of the second
A ghosted parallelogram illustrating that swapping the addition order yields the same resultant
student_actions: Slide the second vector until its tail connects to the first vector's tip to form the chain
Reveal the resultant arrow and read off its magnitude and direction
Swap the two vectors' order and confirm the resultant is unchanged

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce vector decomposition along the x- and y-axes and connect magnitude, direction, and components through right-triangle trigonometry.
key_visuals: A single vector overlaid on an x-y coordinate grid
Dashed horizontal and vertical projection lines forming a right triangle beneath the vector
Labels showing the component lengths alongside the sine/cosine relationships to the vector's magnitude and angle
student_actions: Rotate the vector and watch the horizontal and vertical components stretch and shrink
Match the displayed component values against the trig relationships (magnitude times cosine and sine of the angle)
Reconstruct the original vector from its two components to confirm the decomposition

scenes.brief_purpose: Bridge abstract vectors to projectile motion by treating a projectile's initial velocity as a vector to be decomposed into horizontal and vertical parts.
key_visuals: A launcher on the ground with a velocity arrow pointing along the launch angle
The velocity arrow splitting into a horizontal component arrow and a vertical component arrow
A control panel with dials for launch angle and initial speed
student_actions: Set an initial speed and launch angle and observe the resulting velocity vector
Watch the velocity vector decompose into its horizontal and vertical components and note their values
Predict which component will stay constant and which will change once the projectile is in flight

scenes.scene_name: Independence of Horizontal and Vertical Motion
scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate the central insight that horizontal velocity stays constant while vertical velocity changes under gravity, and that the two motions are independent.
key_visuals: A launched projectile whose horizontal component arrow stays a fixed length throughout flight
A vertical component arrow that shrinks during ascent, vanishes at the peak, and grows downward during descent
Two synchronized 'shadow' markers tracing the motion separately on a horizontal track and a vertical track
student_actions: Launch the projectile and watch the horizontal and vertical component arrows evolve during flight
Pause the motion at the peak to confirm the vertical component is zero while the horizontal component is unchanged
Compare the vertical shadow's accelerating motion with the horizontal shadow's steady motion

scenes.brief_purpose: Let students experiment with launch parameters to see how angle and speed determine trajectory shape, range, and maximum height, and to recognize the parabolic path as the combination of the two motions.
key_visuals: A full parabolic trajectory arc traced across the AR scene
On-screen measurements of range and maximum height that update with each launch
Faint overlaid arcs from previous launches for comparison
student_actions: Vary the launch angle at fixed speed and record how range and maximum height change
Find the angle that produces the greatest range and compare complementary angles that yield the same range
Increase the initial speed and observe how the entire trajectory scales

scenes.brief_purpose: Assess and consolidate learning by asking students to predict outcomes and hit a target using their understanding of components and independent motion.
key_visuals: A target placed at a set distance on the ground
A prediction input for the launch angle and speed needed to reach the target
A summary scoreboard comparing predicted versus actual range and height
student_actions: Predict a launch angle and speed that will land the projectile on the target and enter the values
Launch and compare the actual landing point to the prediction, then adjust and retry as needed
Write a short conclusion explaining how vector decomposition and motion independence guided the successful shot
